note: Extracted from the shipped example public/examples/coldharbour.bundle.json, the study the demo walk of 2026-09-13 produced. Chunk text and every event that is not a proposal, an adjudication or an ontology mutation are dropped; nothing else is changed.

events.title: Mentors stopped reading founder updates within three weeks
events.body: Ravi Patel read three updates in week one, found them to be the same page with the company name changed, and stopped reading them. This happened while you were sitting in the programme, so you watched the stated purpose of the Pitchwright requirement and the mentors' actual behaviour pull apart in real time, not something reconstructed after the fact.

events.title: Ravi's marginal word for Hannah, Gabriel, and Leah
events.body: Hannah got "fine," Gabriel got "solid," and Leah Morgan got "there's something there," the last word arriving only after Ravi dropped the deck and asked what the restaurant actually said when she showed up. She froze, then told him about the kitchen porter, and that's when he leaned in. So the third word is tied to a moment where Ravi went off the script that produced the first two.

events.title: The room as what's left after the tool
events.body: Ravi's own account, offered unprompted between slots: the programme believes the tool made things fair because it made the pages identical, but that just means all he has left to judge on is the room, and the room is not fair, it's who is comfortable being interrupted. This is his explanation for why Leah's off-script recovery moved him and the two clean decks didn't. You're reporting it as his stated view, not yet as your own account of what's driving his ratings.

events.title: "Command of the business" added to the Selection Day sheet
events.body: Chloe Park tells mentors the sheet now has a line for command of the business, and Ravi's reaction, after she leaves, is "that's the room, they've put the room on the sheet." You're recording this as his read that the very quality he just named as unfair, comfort under interruption, is being written into the formal criteria.

events.title: Time-allocation pattern confirmed across mentors, not just Ravi
events.body: Ravi's week-4 slot is the one written up in full, but it's not the only one sat in across ten weeks of two afternoons a week. The same split turns up independently elsewhere: Ethan Brooks notes in the mentors' Slack that Gabriel again ran 25 minutes and Leah got 11 because he had to leave, Olivia replies that she sees the same pattern, and Daniel Kim's slot log puts a number on it, 21 minutes average for introduced founders against 13 for open call.

events.title: Olivia's command scores track founders she already has context on
events.body: Olivia says she stopped reading the decks by week three because they're all the same deck, and that she gives her highest command-of-the-business scores to founders she already had context on, meaning the ones introduced through someone. This comes from interview rather than from sitting in on her slot directly, so it's her own account of what she does, not something watched.

events.title: Coldharbour Launch is the site, not Pitchwright
events.body: Pitchwright is the copilot, the tool that arrived in the programme. Coldharbour Launch is the programme itself, the site of the study, and you were already around it as critical friend before the tool existed. Worth being precise about this going forward so the ontology doesn't end up organized around the tool's name instead of the site where the tool landed.

events.title: Three things true of Coldharbour Launch before you saw any judging
events.body: The board wrote its aim for the copilot down in a January paper, before it went live, so there's a stated intention on record to hold any outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so how heavily a venture used the tool isn't a choice that could confound comparison. And the programme scores every venture on the same sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort already scored on that sheet without the tool in place.

events.title: Critical-friend relationship, unpaid and informal, predates the AI question
events.body: You're in room B2 because you already had standing access to Coldharbour Launch, as an informal critical friend who sits in and feeds back but doesn't score anything and isn't paid. That relationship existed before you had any interest in AI writing tools, and it's the reason you could be there at all when the board licensed Pitchwright. Worth marking as a condition on the whole study: whatever you're seeing is seen from inside a specific, non-evaluative role, not from outside as a neutral observer.

events.title: Convenience sample, access not theory
events.body: You didn't choose Coldharbour Launch from a set of programmes on any theoretical basis. You were already there when Pitchwright got licensed in January, and you recognized what that made possible. You want this written down as a limitation rather than reframed as a deliberate site selection.

events.title: Whether Olivia and Ravi are performing fairness at you
events.body: Because the mentors know exactly who you are and what you're there for, you can't rule out that Olivia's and Ravi's judging behavior is shaped by your presence rather than reflecting what they'd do unwatched. You name this as something you have no clean way to check, not something you've found evidence for or against.

events.title: Panel deliberation invisible; joint score hides individual reasoning
events.body: Selection Day scores for Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs come out of mentors talking to each other, not just filling in a sheet, and what you get afterward is the sheet plus whatever people tell you, not the reasoning as it formed. Any trading or deferring between mentors in that room is invisible to you, and an individual mentor's reasoning is partly folded into a score that's actually joint.

events.title: No visibility into what Pitchwright did inside a founder's writing process
events.body: You have the outputs (one-pagers, decks) and a usage log of which ventures used the tool heavily, but no drafts, no prompts, no record of what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, you're taking her word for the mechanism, not observing it.

events.title: Three output-side proxies for tool-driven convergence
events.body: Before/after cohort comparison on the same programme and template, a dose split on the usage log (heavy vs light users), and phrase-level signatures like "underserved by incumbents" appearing across ventures with no contact. You're explicit these are all measured on the output, none of them touch the drafting process itself, and you're calling this the best available short of the actual drafts and prompts.

events.title: Same phrase across three unconnected ventures in one week
events.body: Olivia noticed three ventures using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week, ventures that never spoke to each other. You note phrase-level repetition like this is hard to explain another way, without yet saying what it would or wouldn't rule out.

events.title: What the within-programme comparisons can and cannot carry
events.body: The site can support four comparisons and no more: this cohort against last year's on the same sheet, introduced against open-call within the cohort, heavy against light tool users from the usage log, and mentors' own accounts of the shift given while it was happening. What none of these four can produce is a counterfactual programme, so the site cannot show that the tool caused the move from page to room rather than merely accompanied it. You'd rather say this plainly than dress it up: a reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.

events.title: One instance = one venture's evaluation across the full twelve weeks
events.body: You're defining the unit you're tracing as the evaluation of a single venture across the cohort, not any smaller or larger grain. It opens at that venture's first office-hours slot, runs through the weekly one-page update and the mid-cohort sheet, and closes when the panel scores it on Selection Day. That's the span any claim about "how judgment forms" has to hold across, start to end, for it to be about this process rather than some other one.

events.title: Eighteen parallel instances, not one programme-wide drift
events.body: The process you're following runs founder by founder, eighteen separate instances in this cohort running in parallel rather than a single process moving across the whole programme at once. The drift you've confirmed across mentors is real, but you're treating it as the condition each instance runs inside, not as the process itself. So the drift explains the air in the room; it isn't what you're tracing when you follow one venture from office hours to Selection Day.

events.title: Weekly office-hours slot as the repeated unit inside an instance
events.body: Inside a single venture's evaluation, the thing that repeats is the office-hours slot: a mentor comes in holding last week's impression, tests it against whatever the founder can do live, writes a word next to the name, and carries that word into the following week. That cycle, impression tested and re-written, is what does the forming and re-forming across the twelve weeks. The written update runs beside it but you're noting it stops being part of that cycle by around week three.

events.title: Shift keyed to mentor's reading dose, not calendar week
events.body: The move from page to room doesn't line up with programme week and doesn't line up with where a given venture sits in its own twelve weeks either. Ravi stopped reading around week two, Olivia around week three, and in both cases what seems to trigger it is having read three or four pages that felt interchangeable, however many weeks that took. So the clock that matters is each mentor's count of updates read, not the calendar and not the venture's sequence.

events.title: Two processes, previously run together
events.body: You'd been describing this as one thing, eighteen ventures moving through twelve weeks to a score, but you now think there are two processes and you'd been sloppy about which one you're actually studying. The venture-level one is the eighteen parallel evaluations ending in a score. The mentor-level one is the attention shift itself, forty mentors, each running on their own exposure to updates, meeting the venture-level process at the weekly office-hours slot. Your tentative read is that the mentor-level shift is the process you're actually studying, and the venture evaluation is the unit that carries its outcome.

events.title: Mentor-level instance runs first read to stated stopping point, one-way
events.body: For the mentor-level process, one instance runs from that mentor's first read of a weekly update to the point they stop reading, and in this cohort it doesn't restart, so it's a short span rather than the full twelve weeks. For Ravi and Olivia that's roughly two to three weeks. You're defining the instance by first-read-to-stopping-point, not by a fixed calendar window.

events.title: Stopping rate noticed, not measured
events.body: You have Ravi saying he read three updates in week one and stopped, and Olivia saying she stopped around week three, both citing the same reason, that the pages were interchangeable. That's a rate in the loose sense, but you're careful to say it isn't a measured dose, since a measured one would need each mentor's reading crossed with which pages they actually read. Nobody logs mentor reading, and you doubt you could reconstruct one honestly, so the page count stays something you noticed rather than something you measured.

events.title: Leah Morgan's week four slot, twenty to three
events.body: Leah delivered her Pitchwright deck as a rehearsed monologue. Ravi let her finish, then told her to forget all that and say what the restaurant had actually said when she turned up. She froze, then told him about the kitchen porter deciding who takes the fat away, and that was the point he leaned forward for the first time in the slot. His note next to her name, "there's something there," was the warmest word he wrote that afternoon, and it came out of the two minutes she was off script.

events.title: Hannah's own printed page, founder-side mirror
events.body: Hannah showed up with her own ugly two-column page she'd printed herself, alongside or instead of the standardised deck. You're reading this as the same finding as Leah's slot but seen from the founder's side: something the founder made outside the tool is what carries the weight in the room.

events.title: Three processes disentangled: shift, in-room evaluation, venture-level accumulation
events.body: What looked like one thing sorts into three. The mentor attention shift is short and one-way, finished for Ravi by week two. The in-room evaluation is what the shift produced: a weekly office-hours slot with its opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, and the word written down, repeating roughly ten times per venture. The venture's twelve-week evaluation is where those weekly words accumulate, landing in the mid-cohort sheet and the Selection Day score. The Leah scene in week four is an instance of the second, not the first, with the first as its origin and the third as where it lands.

events.title: Which process the study is actually tracking
events.body: The object of study is the in-room evaluation, the weekly office-hours instance, not the attention shift that preceded it and not the twelve-week accumulation that follows it. The shift is treated as origin, the venture-level sheet as destination. Anything the study claims should be read as a claim about this middle process specifically, not about the other two.

events.title: Cohort-over-cohort selection rate by prior introduction
events.body: Last cohort, one of three grants went to an introduced founder. This cohort, three of three: Kerbside, Bramble, and Fenwick Labs. This is the comparison you'd point to as the outcome the study is about, and you note it survives the objection that the command line didn't need to exist last time for the pattern to hold. Same programme, same grant, same sheet for four of its five lines.

events.title: Loomly and Tallow diverge on traction and command
events.body: Loomly and Tallow score highest on traction and lowest on command, and you flag this as the result a reviewer should sit up at. You haven't said yet what you think it means, just that it's the pairing in the data that stands out against the rest of the pattern.

events.title: Gap between scored ranking and spoken ranking
events.body: One of your three within-cohort supporting comparisons is the gap between what mentors put on the sheet and what they say in the room or on Slack. Ethan Brooks writes that the pages are all fine and he cannot rank fine against fine. You're holding this as a comparison alongside the introduced-versus-open-call and heavy-versus-light-user comparisons, not yet saying what the gap between stated score and stated difficulty means.

events.title: Chloe's memo dates the abandonment before the fifth line
events.body: The memo's "What we have heard" section has several mentors reporting the updates are uniform and that they're reading less into them, and two saying they no longer read them before office hours. That account puts the abandonment before the fifth line arrived in week seven, and the programme's own record is that the line was written to catch what mentors were already doing. So the ordering isn't something you're reconstructing after the fact, it's what the programme itself says happened.

events.title: Strip the fifth line and rescore on the old four
events.body: If you take the command line out and rescore this cohort on the four lines the last cohort also had, and the introduced founders still come out on top, the effect is bigger than the new line and your claim about abandonment holds more broadly. If they don't, and Loomly and Tallow scoring highest on traction is a hint they might not, then the fifth line is carrying the difference, and what you can claim shrinks to a specific chain: the tool emptied the page, the programme wrote the room onto the sheet, and the sheet did the rest. You haven't run this yet, but it's the test that would tell you which version you're in.

events.title: Two cohorts each side would settle it, and you don't have them
events.body: Even with the strip-test result, you'd want two cohorts before the abandonment and two after to be confident the pattern isn't cohort-specific noise. You're working with one cohort on the new side of the line, so whatever the rescoring shows, it settles the mechanism for this instance without yet settling whether it generalizes.

events.title: Programme's response to an emptied artefact, not tool bias
events.body: If the rescoring goes the way the researcher expects, the account they're now sitting with is that the required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, and the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead of the writing. The criterion it added to compensate is the one that happens to track prior acquaintance. The researcher is explicit that this puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, and that this is narrower than what they set out expecting, but they think it's truer.

events.title: Selection result as outcome, discrimination collapse as mechanism, in that order
events.body: You're splitting the abstract into an outcome and a mechanism, and putting them in a fixed order: selection result first, then mentors' account of why. The selection result is what varied, three of three grants to introduced founders against one of three in the previous cohort, and that's the number the abstract leads with because it's the reason anyone keeps reading. The discrimination-collapse reports aren't a second outcome sitting alongside it, they're the explanation for why the first number moved.

events.title: Outcome without mechanism is correlation, mechanism without outcome is complaint
events.body: You said the two pieces need each other to mean anything: the selection result alone gives you a correlation between a tool and a cohort, and the mentors' account alone gives you an interesting complaint. It's only holding both, the number and the reason mentors give for the number, that gets you something worth calling a finding. You're naming this as the reason the grounds half of the claim isn't decoration.

events.title: Discrimination-collapse claim recurs across interview, Slack, and memo
events.body: You can evidence the "instrument stopped discriminating" claim in three separate registers: mentors saying it to you in interview, mentors saying it to each other on Slack, and mentors saying it to Chloe in the memo that changed the scoring sheet. You're flagging this as the part of the mechanism claim you can back most solidly, because it shows up unprompted across three different audiences rather than only in the setting where you asked for it.

events.title: Census at venture level, sample at office-hours and interview level
events.body: The venture is a census, all eighteen ventures' updates, usage logs and Selection Day sheets, so the introduced/open-call split (roughly a third to two thirds) is covered in full at that level. The office-hours slot is a different unit and a sample, about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks, and the interview set is smaller still, seven founders picked to fill cells. So whatever the venture-level data can support on its own, the same comparison run through office-hours observation or interviews is resting on much thinner numbers, and I shouldn't let the census cover for the sample when I write this up.

events.title: Interview cells crossed on route-in and use-intensity are one or two deep
events.body: I picked seven founders to fill cells crossing introduced/open-call with heavy/light Pitchwright use: Hannah and Leah for open call, Gabriel, Samuel and Natalie for introduced. Crossed on one dimension the groups are workable, but crossed on both at once each cell holds only one or two founders. I'd rather flag that thinness now than let the interview material carry more weight than seven people split into four cells can hold.

events.title: Mentor confounded with cell for introduced/heavy-use founders
events.body: The founders who are introduced and heavy-use are mostly Ravi's founders in your observed slots, so you can't tell whether what you're seeing is a mentor effect or a route-in/use-intensity effect. Ravi's week-two shift (laptop closed, one word per name) is something you watched directly; Olivia's week-three shift you only have secondhand from her interview; Ethan's account of still reading and not being able to rank fine against fine you only have from Slack. Three different evidence types standing in for what should be the same kind of observation across mentors, and you can't yet separate the mentor from the cell.

events.title: Olivia and Ethan's slots, recalled split by route-in and use
events.body: Uncounted so far, but from memory: Olivia's slots skew open-call because she took the Tuesday group and that's where the open-call founders mostly landed, and Ethan's slots are the ones he cut short. This is recall, not a tally, and you're treating it as provisional until you run the count against the fieldnotes and usage log. If it holds once counted, watching Olivia and Ethan more doesn't rebalance the introduced/open-call or heavy/light split, it just gives you more of the same skew.

events.title: Introduced-plus-light-user cell may be empty in this cohort
events.body: The cell that stays empty either way, introduced founder paired with light tool use, may simply have no occupant this cohort. You're not sure a founder exists who sits in it. If so, any claim your design makes about that cell can't be tested here regardless of how the count comes out, and that's a limit on the comparison, not a finding about it.

events.title: Evaluators judging entrepreneurial potential from a founder's communication will let style cues, not just underlying venture substance, drive their assessment of scalability and long-term growth.
events.body:
Where the expectation holds: The authors say this holds in investor evaluation of founder pitches and tie the mechanism specifically to gender-linked linguistic patterns, not to network access or prior contact.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them
events.body: Multiple mentors independently report the weekly Pitchwright updates have become interchangeable and they've stopped reading them, which is the opposite of what a legibility tool is supposed to produce. Olivia Ward says "They are all the same deck. Not similar, the same" and names the repeated phrase "underserved by incumbents" [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Ravi Patel says he read three in week one and stopped [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], and Chloe Park's own memo confirms "several mentors report... they are reading less into them" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Introduced founders get longer office-hours slots
events.body: Daniel Kim's slot log shows introduced founders averaging 21 minutes against 13 for open-call founders across weeks 3 to 6 [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], and this shows up live in the fieldnote where Gabriel's slot runs 24 minutes against a scheduled 15 while Hannah and Leah get compressed slots [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Ethan Brooks names the same pattern about himself: "Gabriel's slot ran 25 mins again. Leah got 11 because I had to leave. Not proud of that" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]].

events.title: Tool removed writing as a signal, mentors substituted room performance
events.body: Olivia Ward gives the clearest first-person account of the mechanism: the pages became decent for everyone, "the page stopped telling me anything, and I went back to the thing the page was supposed to stop me relying on," which she names as "whether they sound like someone I'd back" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Ravi Patel states the same causal chain to Marcus directly: "It made the pages identical, so now all I've got is the room. And the room is not fair, mate, the room is who's comfortable being interrupted" [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. Chloe Park's memo formalizes this substitution by adding a "command of the business" line scored from office-hours contact [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Command-of-business score tracks prior exposure to being interrupted, not venture quality
events.body: Olivia admits she scored command highest for founders she already had context on "because I knew what they'd been doing before the programme, so I could tell when an answer was real" [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]]. Gabriel, a former bank product manager, says being interrupted "is how meetings work" and endorses the command line as testing the right thing [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while Hannah Foster, a former teacher, says interruption "reads as not having an answer" for her [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. This suggests the command score may be measuring rehearsed comfort with a particular conversational style rather than command of the venture itself.

events.title: It's the door, not the deck
events.body: Gabriel offers a competing account of what actually drives the disparity: not the tool's removal of writing as signal, but pre-existing relationships between mentors and introduced founders. Asked whether Hannah would get what he gets if she used the tool identically, he says "No. Not because of the tool. Because Ravi doesn't know anyone she's worked with. It's not the deck, it's the door" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83098d5e]]. This locates the cause in the introduction network itself rather than in anything the tool changed.

events.title: Hannah Foster keeps two documents each week
events.body: Hannah describes maintaining the required Pitchwright one-pager for the programme alongside a self-made two-column page of "the numbers and what people actually said to me" that she actually uses in the room, because office-hours questions are "never on the page" [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. This is directly corroborated in the fieldnote, where Ravi waves away her laptop and looks instead at the page she printed herself [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]].

events.title: Selection Day grants went entirely to introduced founders
events.body: Daniel Kim's appended note records that all three Selection Day grants (Kerbside, Bramble, Fenwick Labs) went to founders who came in through a mentor introduction, while the two highest-traction open-call ventures, Loomly and Tallow, scored lowest on the new command line [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. The note also flags that last cohort, before the tool and before the command line, one of three grants went to an introduced founder, an implicit before/after contrast.

events.title: Ravi runs office hours with the laptop closed
events.body: The fieldnote records Ravi Patel keeping a printed list of eighteen venture names and writing one word next to each after a slot, having stopped reading the Pitchwright updates after week one because "they were the same page with the company name changed" [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]]. His one-word notes across three consecutive slots ("fine", "solid", "there's something there") are the only visible trace of his scoring process in the field record [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]].

events.title: Gabriel endorses the very asymmetry that disadvantages him least
events.body: Gabriel states the command-of-business line is "what the programme should be testing, and it's what they are testing now" [[chunk:48c3ba91-ac43-48d1-9089-28fe91d4c87d]], while also acknowledging in the same interview that the tool "cleared the page out of the way so the room is all that's left, which suits me. I'm not going to pretend otherwise" [[chunk:da5a5470-8def-41b3-b088-d9ba83084d5e]]. His endorsement of the fairness of the current arrangement sits alongside his explicit self-interest in it, and the material doesn't resolve whether his account of what the programme "should" test is a genuine belief or a rationalization.

events.title: Chloe Park frames the command line as making explicit what mentors already do
events.body: Chloe's memo describes the new scoring line as making "explicit what mentors say they are already doing in the room" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], treating the room-based judgment as a pre-existing, presumably legitimate practice being formalized. This framing sits in tension with Ravi's characterization of the same change, "They've put the room on the sheet" [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], which reads as diagnosing a problem rather than endorsing a fix, and with Olivia's own admission that her room-based judgments are shaped by prior familiarity rather than what happens in the fifteen minutes [[chunk:533ae601-1f69-4b1b-b9f9-65271b196667]].

events.title: Leah Morgan's room opened, her command score didn't follow
events.body: The one moment in your week-4 fieldnote where Ravi leans forward for an open-call founder is Leah's, when the question stops being about the page and she tells the kitchen-porter story. He writes "there's something there," warmer than the "fine" he gives Hannah [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. But her command score still came out low, so the room opening didn't carry through to the score the way your account would predict. You're calling this a near miss rather than a counter-case, and I'd leave it exactly that unsettled: it doesn't overturn the pattern, but it isn't absorbed by it either.

events.title: Pattern currently rests on two founders and one aggregate line
events.body: Right now the claim that introduced founders score high on command and open-call founders score low draws on Hannah, Gabriel, and Daniel's note that Loomly and Tallow sit lowest on command and highest on traction [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You haven't read the command line for the other fifteen ventures individually, and you said yourself one of the three grant winners could have scored poorly on command and won on team or market. Until that tabulation is done, the pattern holds at the level of two founders and an aggregate, not a checked census.

events.title: Hannah Foster's bind anchors the paper, not a mentor's dilemma
events.body: Olivia, Ravi, and Chloe are all caught between the tool and what it costs, but each of them can name the trade out loud and keeps the job either way, Ravi can say the room isn't fair and carry on running it the next day [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Hannah cannot name it and cannot get out of it: she is required to file the Pitchwright page, Daniel checks that she has, she knows nobody reads it, so she writes a second page by hand for the room, complying and routing around the compliance in the same week [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. That's what should anchor the paper, a bind someone is living rather than a dilemma someone with standing is observing.

events.title: Leah Morgan as the same bind, minus the workaround
events.body: Leah Morgan is in Hannah's position, required to file the tool's page, judged on something the page doesn't carry, but she hasn't built the second document Hannah built for herself. Without that workaround she delivers the Pitchwright deck straight, as a rehearsed monologue, and only breaks from it when Ravi forces the question the page can't answer [[chunk:28e11f01-cc47-4ee3-87b2-0596e8a144d2]]. She's the control case for what the bind looks like with no artefact routing around it.

events.title: Hannah's diagnosis has no venue that counts as input
events.body: She said it to me in a cafe, off the record. At Coldharbour, the weekly update is the channel, and it's the channel she's describing the problem with. Office hours are fifteen minutes of being interrupted about parent pricing, not a place to make the argument [[chunk:8daaf22d-d44d-4ed4-b2b8-5fe0d2123984]]. The Selection Day sheet has no line for it either, so she can state the trap precisely and still have nowhere at the programme to put the statement, which is why it comes out as a second sheet of paper instead of a complaint [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]].

events.title: Hannah's ask is two things the programme can't grant together
events.body: Read the pages, or stop pretending the pages are the point, either one, not both [[chunk:6da43e6d-6dd5-4b69-ab42-ea802ed3321c]]. Granting the second half means conceding, within a single term, that the board paper's stated aim (level the field so mentors judge the venture, not the writing) was wrong. That's the bind underneath her bind, and it's my current best sense of why nothing moves, though I haven't got past naming it that way.

events.title: Chloe's Slack admission becomes the memo's fairness claim
events.body: In week 5, after Daniel posts the slot log, Chloe writes in the mentors' Slack channel that she is proposing the command line "so we are at least scoring the room openly rather than pretending we score the deck" [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]]. That is her naming the contradiction herself, informally, before any memo exists. By the week-7 memo the same move is described as making "explicit what mentors say they are already doing" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]], the same fact with the word "pretending" gone and the board paper's fairness aim left standing, unretracted.

events.title: Board's leveling expectation for the shared writing tool
events.body: The board's January paper commits to a specific claim: mentors couldn't tell whether the venture or the writing was being rated, and a shared writing assistant required of every founder levels this, so mentors will be judging comparable documents for the first time [[chunk:f87f37d1-6bf1-4222-8416-cc791b5ef700]]. You name this as the strongest and most documented expectation held by anyone in the setting, and the one your case breaks. You don't yet say what replaces it, only that this is the expectation whose failure the paper turns on.

events.title: Chloe's week-five defense: uniform pages mean the tool is working
events.body: In the mentors channel, Chloe answers Olivia and Ethan's complaint that the pages are all "fine" and can't be ranked against each other by saying that's the tool working, since it was brought in so the writing wouldn't be the thing being ranked [[chunk:d6d50f0b-9d17-4537-be6e-96abc3e3f3a1]]. You say she's right on the tool's own terms, and wrong about what follows, without yet specifying what that further wrong thing is. This sits as a live alternative reading of the same fact (uniform pages) that you and she draw opposite conclusions from.

events.title: Uniform pages stop mentors from reading them
events.body: Multiple mentors independently report the weekly Pitchwright updates have become interchangeable and they've stopped reading them, which is the opposite of what a legibility tool is supposed to produce. Olivia Ward says "They are all the same deck. Not similar, the same" and names the repeated phrase "underserved by incumbents" [[chunk:5424432e-5339-4bc4-89b7-d146dfac7507]]. Ravi Patel says he read three in week one and stopped [[chunk:f98ca04f-f097-4baf-afa8-c5b90e832ac3]], and Chloe Park's own memo confirms "several mentors report... they are reading less into them" [[chunk:092ca834-03bb-4eea-8682-bc9c84fadd04]].

events.title: Site warrant: aim on record before the tool, use required of all eighteen, same sheet across two cohorts
events.body: The board wrote its aim for the copilot down in a January paper, before it went live, so there's a stated intention on record to hold any outcome against. Use was required of all eighteen ventures, so how heavily a venture used the tool isn't a choice that could confound comparison. And the programme scores every venture on the same sheet at a fixed moment, Selection Day, with a previous cohort already scored on that sheet without the tool in place.

events.title: Critical-friend relationship, unpaid and informal, predates the AI question
events.body: You're in room B2 because you already had standing access to Coldharbour Launch, as an informal critical friend who sits in and feeds back but doesn't score anything and isn't paid. That relationship existed before you had any interest in AI writing tools, and it's the reason you could be there at all when the board licensed Pitchwright. Worth marking as a condition on the whole study: whatever you're seeing is seen from inside a specific, non-evaluative role, not from outside as a neutral observer.

events.title: Panel deliberation invisible; joint score hides individual reasoning
events.body: Selection Day scores for Kerbside, Bramble and Fenwick Labs come out of mentors talking to each other, not just filling in a sheet, and what you get afterward is the sheet plus whatever people tell you, not the reasoning as it formed. Any trading or deferring between mentors in that room is invisible to you, and an individual mentor's reasoning is partly folded into a score that's actually joint.

events.title: No visibility into what Pitchwright did inside a founder's writing process
events.body: You have the outputs (one-pagers, decks) and a usage log of which ventures used the tool heavily, but no drafts, no prompts, no record of what a founder pasted in against what the tool handed back. So when Hannah says the first page made her sound like she knew what she was doing, you're taking her word for the mechanism, not observing it.

events.title: Same phrase across three unconnected ventures in one week
events.body: Olivia noticed three ventures using "underserved by incumbents" in the same week, ventures that never spoke to each other. You note phrase-level repetition like this is hard to explain another way, without yet saying what it would or wouldn't rule out.

events.title: What the within-programme comparisons can and cannot carry
events.body: The site can support four comparisons and no more: this cohort against last year's on the same sheet, introduced against open-call within the cohort, heavy against light tool users from the usage log, and mentors' own accounts of the shift given while it was happening. What none of these four can produce is a counterfactual programme, so the site cannot show that the tool caused the move from page to room rather than merely accompanied it. You'd rather say this plainly than dress it up: a reviewer who wants causal identification should not be reading this paper.

events.title: Shift keyed to mentor's reading dose, not calendar week
events.body: The move from page to room doesn't line up with programme week and doesn't line up with where a given venture sits in its own twelve weeks either. Ravi stopped reading around week two, Olivia around week three, and in both cases what seems to trigger it is having read three or four pages that felt interchangeable, however many weeks that took. So the clock that matters is each mentor's count of updates read, not the calendar and not the venture's sequence.

events.title: Stopping rate noticed, not measured
events.body: You have Ravi saying he read three updates in week one and stopped, and Olivia saying she stopped around week three, both citing the same reason, that the pages were interchangeable. That's a rate in the loose sense, but you're careful to say it isn't a measured dose, since a measured one would need each mentor's reading crossed with which pages they actually read. Nobody logs mentor reading, and you doubt you could reconstruct one honestly, so the page count stays something you noticed rather than something you measured.

events.title: Leah Morgan's week four slot, twenty to three
events.body: Leah delivered her Pitchwright deck as a rehearsed monologue. Ravi let her finish, then told her to forget all that and say what the restaurant had actually said when she turned up. She froze, then told him about the kitchen porter deciding who takes the fat away, and that was the point he leaned forward for the first time in the slot. His note next to her name, "there's something there," was the warmest word he wrote that afternoon, and it came out of the two minutes she was off script.

events.title: Three processes disentangled: shift, in-room evaluation, venture-level accumulation
events.body: What looked like one thing sorts into three. The mentor attention shift is short and one-way, finished for Ravi by week two. The in-room evaluation is what the shift produced: a weekly office-hours slot with its opening, unscripted probe, interruptions, and the word written down, repeating roughly ten times per venture. The venture's twelve-week evaluation is where those weekly words accumulate, landing in the mid-cohort sheet and the Selection Day score. The Leah scene in week four is an instance of the second, not the first, with the first as its origin and the third as where it lands.

events.title: Which process the study is actually tracking
events.body: The object of study is the in-room evaluation, the weekly office-hours instance, not the attention shift that preceded it and not the twelve-week accumulation that follows it. The shift is treated as origin, the venture-level sheet as destination. Anything the study claims should be read as a claim about this middle process specifically, not about the other two.

events.title: Mentor reactivity cannot be ruled out: they know what I am watching for
events.body: Because the mentors know exactly who you are and what you're there for, you can't rule out that Olivia's and Ravi's judging behavior is shaped by your presence rather than reflecting what they'd do unwatched. You name this as something you have no clean way to check, not something you've found evidence for or against.

events.title: Chloe's memo dates the abandonment before the fifth line
events.body: The memo's "What we have heard" section has several mentors reporting the updates are uniform and that they're reading less into them, and two saying they no longer read them before office hours. That account puts the abandonment before the fifth line arrived in week seven, and the programme's own record is that the line was written to catch what mentors were already doing. So the ordering isn't something you're reconstructing after the fact, it's what the programme itself says happened.

events.title: Strip the fifth line and rescore on the old four
events.body: If you take the command line out and rescore this cohort on the four lines the last cohort also had, and the introduced founders still come out on top, the effect is bigger than the new line and your claim about abandonment holds more broadly. If they don't, and Loomly and Tallow scoring highest on traction is a hint they might not, then the fifth line is carrying the difference, and what you can claim shrinks to a specific chain: the tool emptied the page, the programme wrote the room onto the sheet, and the sheet did the rest. You haven't run this yet, but it's the test that would tell you which version you're in.

events.title: Programme's response to an emptied artefact, not tool bias
events.body: If the rescoring goes the way the researcher expects, the account they're now sitting with is that the required writing tool emptied the artefact of information, and the programme responded by scoring the interaction instead of the writing. The criterion it added to compensate is the one that happens to track prior acquaintance. The researcher is explicit that this puts the causal weight on the programme's response rather than on the tool, and that this is narrower than what they set out expecting, but they think it's truer.

events.title: Discrimination-collapse claim recurs across interview, Slack, and memo
events.body: You can evidence the "instrument stopped discriminating" claim in three separate registers: mentors saying it to you in interview, mentors saying it to each other on Slack, and mentors saying it to Chloe in the memo that changed the scoring sheet. You're flagging this as the part of the mechanism claim you can back most solidly, because it shows up unprompted across three different audiences rather than only in the setting where you asked for it.

events.title: Census at venture level, sample at office-hours and interview level
events.body: The venture is a census, all eighteen ventures' updates, usage logs and Selection Day sheets, so the introduced/open-call split (roughly a third to two thirds) is covered in full at that level. The office-hours slot is a different unit and a sample, about thirty slots across four mentors over ten weeks, and the interview set is smaller still, seven founders picked to fill cells. So whatever the venture-level data can support on its own, the same comparison run through office-hours observation or interviews is resting on much thinner numbers, and I shouldn't let the census cover for the sample when I write this up.

events.title: Mentor confounded with cell for introduced/heavy-use founders
events.body: The founders who are introduced and heavy-use are mostly Ravi's founders in your observed slots, so you can't tell whether what you're seeing is a mentor effect or a route-in/use-intensity effect. Ravi's week-two shift (laptop closed, one word per name) is something you watched directly; Olivia's week-three shift you only have secondhand from her interview; Ethan's account of still reading and not being able to rank fine against fine you only have from Slack. Three different evidence types standing in for what should be the same kind of observation across mentors, and you can't yet separate the mentor from the cell.

events.title: Introduced-plus-light-user cell may be empty in this cohort
events.body: The cell that stays empty either way, introduced founder paired with light tool use, may simply have no occupant this cohort. You're not sure a founder exists who sits in it. If so, any claim your design makes about that cell can't be tested here regardless of how the count comes out, and that's a limit on the comparison, not a finding about it.

events.title: Evaluators judging entrepreneurial potential from a founder's communication will let style cues, not just underlying venture substance, drive their assessment of scalability and long-term growth.
events.body:
Where the expectation holds: The authors say this holds in investor evaluation of founder pitches and tie the mechanism specifically to gender-linked linguistic patterns, not to network access or prior contact.

Command score tracks founders' theory of what interruption means
events.body: On this account, Gabriel and Hannah aren't at different levels of practice with being cut off, they're running different theories about what a cut-off signals. Gabriel's professional norm codes an interruption as a colleague testing your reasoning, so he answers through it; Hannah's codes it as a verdict that she's already failed, so she folds. For this to beat your comfort-with-interruption explanation, you'd need to see founders who get plenty of exposure to interruption during the programme and still score low because they never stop reading it as a verdict, while someone with little exposure but who's talked through what the interruption is for jumps straight to a high score. That would tell you it's the founder's belief about the interruption doing the work, not how many times they've sat through one, which is different from saying command score may track rehearsed comfort with interruption rather than command of the venture.
